source.title: Do Transformers Learn What Theory Predicts? Knowledge Representation-Guided Mechanistic Verification via Causal Abstraction
source.authors: Chang Lu; Renate A. Schmidt; Yi-Zheng Zhao

record.file_problem: None; the supplied text contains the full paper.
record.tranche_reason: Tests delayed generalization on a different small algorithmic task, binary increment, and uses causal-alignment measures to examine the learned computation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own binary-increment grokking results and mechanistic-alignment results. Mentioned prior-work results are not included. The text says data fractions α=0.3 and α=0.7 were examined at n=16 but gives no outcomes for those settings.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own grokking run on a new small algorithmic task (binary increment). The run shows memorization, then a delay, then perfect test accuracy. It tracks a circuit-specific causal-alignment measure (DAS-IIA) and weight norm through training, which bears on V2. A weight-decay ablation bears on V5, and converged-circuit identification across bit widths and seeds bears on V6. It is not one of the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the two-layer Transformer implements the three-stage B-RASP increment circuit, with wrong-specification controls at chance and SAEs recovering matching features. They also conclude that this structure emerges as a sharp phase transition during grokking rather than gradually, while weight norm declines earlier and gradually and so cannot show what changes. They add that parameter-matched RNNs and SSMs fail to generalize.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a binary-increment task rather than modular arithmetic, with a two-layer Transformer, weight decay, prolonged training, and a mechanistic-alignment analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported alignment depends on component location: Bprev is strongest at L1-attn, Cin at L1-MLP, and Yout at L2-MLP. Removing weight decay lowers IIAmin to 0.53; a one-layer ablation gives IIAmin = 0.61. DAS threshold conclusions are reported as robust to thresholds 0.90 and 0.99, with different pass rates.
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Principles of Knowledge Representation and Reasoning (KR), 2026
record.problems: The main training results use 5 seeds. For n=20 and n=24, the evaluation pool is a uniform sample of 50,000 pairs rather than the complete dataset. Several ablation outcomes are reported only inline, and the text does not provide separate grokking-gap values for every bit width.
record.rows_left_out: No additional relevant reported results omitted. The paper mentions further ablations and decrement results but does not provide all their numerical outcomes in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks. α=0.3 and 0.7 are said to be run at n=16, but no outcomes are given. The gap grows with n, but the training-set size also grows with n, so this is not a dataset-size test.
Fourier algorithms, and later removal of memorizing components (no memorization-circuit measure).
Entire version: no non-algorithmic data, initialization-scale or lazy/rich manipulation.
Entire version: no LLM pretraining or realistic-data fine-tuning.
Circuit efficiency comparison, critical dataset size, ungrokking.
Algorithms under different architectures or broad hyperparameter variation; only one recipe, 5 seeds, varying n.
Entire version: no optimizer or floating-point/softmax controls.

missing.what: Parameter-matched LSTM, GRU and Mamba memorize the training set but never generalize within 100k steps (e.g., LSTM .07 at n=16). This bears on whether delayed generalization holds across architectures.
Test accuracy and grokking outcome for α=0.3 and α=0.7 at n=16. The setup says these were run but the text gives no results, which is needed for V1's dataset-size dependence.
Test accuracy / whether grokking occurs with λ=0 and with ℓ=1. Only IIAmin is reported for these ablations.
n=16 memorization step ~1,800 and grokking step ~18,600, from Figure 2a. These place the IIA transition relative to the generalization step.

record.verdict_notes: The gap grows with n, but at fixed α the training set grows with n (2^n·0.5). This cannot test V1's 'smaller training set, longer delay' part; if anything it is confounded by task difficulty. On V2, the circuit-specific trajectory runs against gradual formation, but the task-agnostic weight-norm measure still anticipates the jump, hence two labels. Many component-level rows (r27–r36) were mislabelled partial or absent; they are localization details, not version effects.

versions.untested_parts: The task is binary increment rather than modular arithmetic. The text does not provide a per-bit-width training-set-size sweep sufficient to test whether smaller training sets increase the delay.
The study tests whether B-RASP variables are encoded and how their alignment changes during training. It does not test Fourier algorithms or whether memorizing components are removed later.
No non-algorithmic data, initialization-scale sweep, or lazy-to-rich transition test is reported.
No LLM pretraining or realistic-data fine-tuning is studied.
The study reports an ablation without weight decay and discusses regularization-driven simplification, but does not test circuit efficiency, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below such a size.

The same prescribed circuit is checked across bit widths and seeds in one Transformer setup. The study does not compare algorithms learned under different architectures or broad hyperparameter choices.
No adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point/softmax artifact control is reported.
